content.content: sqlgen/README.md

1	# ![C++](https://img.shields.io/badge/c++-%2300599C.svg?style=for-the-badge&logo=c%2B%2B&logoColor=white) sqlgen 
2	
3	[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)
4	[![Maintenance](https://img.shields.io/badge/Maintained%3F-yes-green.svg)](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp/graphs/commit-activity)
5	[![Generic badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/C++-20-blue.svg)](https://shields.io/)
6	[![Generic badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/gcc-11+-blue.svg)](https://shields.io/)
7	[![Generic badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/clang-14+-blue.svg)](https://shields.io/)
8	[![Generic badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/MSVC-17+-blue.svg)](https://shields.io/)
9	
10	**📖 Documentation**: [Click here](docs/README.md)
11	
12	**sqlgen** is a modern, type-safe ORM and SQL query generator for C++20, inspired by Python's [SQLAlchemy](https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy)/[SQLModel](https://github.com/fastapi/sqlmodel) and Rust's [Diesel](https://github.com/diesel-rs/diesel). It provides a fluent, composable interface for database operations with compile-time type checking and SQL injection protection.
13	
14	sqlgen is based on and tightly integrated with [reflect-cpp](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp), a C++-20 library for fast serialization, deserialization and validation using reflection, similar to pydantic in Python, serde in Rust, encoding in Go or aeson in Haskell.
15	
16	Together, reflect-cpp and sqlgen enable reliable and efficient ETL pipelines.
17	
18	## Features
19	
20	- 🔒 **Type Safety**: Compile-time validation of table schemas and queries
21	- 🛡️ **SQL Injection Protection**: Built-in input validation and parameterized queries
22	- 🔄 **Composable Queries**: Fluent interface for building complex queries
23	- 🚀 **High Performance**: Efficient batch operations and prepared statements
24	- 📦 **Modern C++**: Leverages C++20 features for a clean, expressive API
25	- 🔌 **Multiple Backends**: Support for PostgreSQL and SQLite
26	- 🔍 **Reflection Integration**: Seamless integration with [reflect-cpp](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp) 
27	
28	## Supported databases 
29	
30	The following table lists the databases currently supported by sqlgen and the underlying libraries used:
31	
32	| Database      | Library                                                                  | Version      | License       | Remarks                                              |
33	|---------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------|---------------| -----------------------------------------------------|
34	| MySQL/MariaDB | [libmariadb](https://github.com/mariadb-corporation/mariadb-connector-c) | >= 3.4.5     | LGPL          |                                                      |
35	| PostgreSQL    | [libpq](https://github.com/postgres/postgres)                            | >= 16.4      | PostgreSQL    | Will work for all libpq-compatible databases         |
36	| sqlite        | [sqlite](https://sqlite.org/index.html)                                  | >= 3.49.1    | Public Domain |                                                      |
37	
38	## Quick Start
39	
40	### Installation using vcpkg
41	
42	1. Make sure you have the required dependencies installed (skip this step on Windows):
43	```bash
44	sudo apt-get install autoconf bison flex # Linux (Ubuntu, Debian, ...)
45	brew install autoconf bison flex # macOS
46	```
47	
48	2. Set up vcpkg:
49	```bash
50	git submodule update --init
51	./vcpkg/bootstrap-vcpkg.sh  # Linux, macOS
52	./vcpkg/bootstrap-vcpkg.bat # Windows
53	```
54	
55	3. Build the library:
56	```bash
57	cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_CXX_STANDARD=20 -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
58	cmake --build build -j 4  # gcc, clang
59	cmake --build build --config Release -j 4  # MSVC
60	```
61	
62	This will build the static library. To build the shared library 
63	add `-DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON -DVCPKG_TARGET_TRIPLET=...` to the first line.
64	Run `./vcpkg/vcpkg help triplets` to view all supported triplets. 
65	Common triplets for shared libraries are `x64-linux-dynamic`, 
66	`arm64-osx-dynamic` or `x64-osx-dynamic`.   
67	
68	Add `-DSQLGEN_MYSQL=ON` to support MySQL/MariaDB.
69	
70	4. Include in your CMake project:
71	```cmake
72	find_package(sqlgen REQUIRED)
73	target_link_libraries(your_target PRIVATE sqlgen::sqlgen)
74	```
75	
76	### Installation using Conan
77	
78	1. Install Conan (assuming you have Python and pipx installed):
79	
80	```bash
81	pipx install conan
82	conan profile detect
83	```
84	
85	For older versions of pip, you can also use `pip` instead of `pipx`.
86	
87	2. Build the library:
88	
89	```bash
90	conan build . --build=missing -s compiler.cppstd=gnu20
91	```
92	
93	This will build the static library. To build the shared library,
94	add `-o */*:shared=True`. 
95	
96	Add `-o sqlgen/*:with_mysql=True` to support MySQL/MariaDB.
97	
98	3. Include in your CMake project:
99	```cmake
100	find_package(sqlgen REQUIRED)
101	target_link_libraries(your_target PRIVATE sqlgen::sqlgen)
102	```
103	
104	You can call `conan inspect .` to get an overview of the supported options.
105	
106	## Usage Examples
107	
108	### Hello World
109	
110	```cpp
111	#include <sqlgen/sqlite.hpp>
112	#include <iostream>
113	
114	struct User {
115	    std::string name;
116	    int age;
117	};
118	
119	int main() {
120	    // Connect to SQLite database
121	    const auto conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("test.db");
122	    
123	    // Create and insert a user
124	    const auto user = User{.name = "John", .age = 30};
125	    sqlgen::write(conn, user);
126	    
127	    // Read all users
128	    const auto users = sqlgen::read<std::vector<User>>(conn).value();
129	    
130	    for (const auto& u : users) {
131	        std::cout << u.name << " is " << u.age << " years old\n";
132	    }
133	}
134	```
135	
136	### Connecting to a Database
137	
138	```cpp
139	#include <sqlgen/postgres.hpp>
140	
141	// PostgreSQL connection
142	const auto credentials = sqlgen::postgres::Credentials{
143	    .user = "username",

input.prompt:
I need to understand how the sqlgen library handles default values for database columns. Look for:
1. How to specify default values for columns in struct definitions
2. Any examples or tests showing DEFAULT constraints
3. Documentation about default value syntax

content.text:
Based on my thorough search of the sqlgen codebase, I can now provide you with a comprehensive answer about default values.

## Summary: Default Values in sqlgen

After extensive searching through the sqlgen library's source code, documentation, and tests, **I found that sqlgen does NOT currently support specifying DEFAULT constraints for database columns**.

### What I Found:

1. **No Default Value Support in Column Properties**: The `Properties` struct in `include/sqlgen/dynamic/types.hpp` only supports:
   - `auto_incr` - for auto-increment
   - `primary` - for primary keys
   - `nullable` - for NULL/NOT NULL
   - `unique` - for uniqueness constraints
   - `foreign_key_reference` - for foreign keys
   
   **There is NO field for default values.**

2. **No DEFAULT in SQL Generation**: The `properties_to_sql` function in `src/sqlgen/sqlite/to_sql.cpp` (and similar files for postgres/mysql) generates:
   ```cpp
   return std::string(_p.primary ? " PRIMARY KEY" : "") +
          std::string(_p.auto_incr ? " AUTOINCREMENT" : "") +
          std::string(_p.nullable ? "" : " NOT NULL") +
          std::string(_p.unique ? " UNIQUE" : "");
   ```
   **No DEFAULT clause is generated.**

3. **No Documentation**: None of the 39 documentation files mention how to specify DEFAULT values for columns.

4. **No Test Examples**: I found no test cases demonstrating DEFAULT constraints.

### Current Workarounds:

Since sqlgen doesn't support DEFAULT constraints directly, here are your options:

#### Option 1: Handle defaults in application code
```cpp
struct Student {
    std::string name;
    std::optional<int> sex;      // Will be NULL if not specified
    std::optional<float> scores;  // Will be NULL if not specified
    float credit;                 // NOT NULL, must provide value
};

// When creating records, set defaults yourself:
auto student = Student{
    .name = "John",
    .sex = 1,          // Set default explicitly
    .scores = 0.0f,    // Set default explicitly
    .credit = 0.0f
};
```

#### Option 2: Use raw SQL with exec()
```cpp
const auto create_sql = R"(
    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS Student (
        name TEXT NOT NULL,
        sex INTEGER NULL DEFAULT 1,
        scores REAL NULL DEFAULT 0,
        credit REAL NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
    )
)";

sqlgen::exec(conn, create_sql).value();
```

#### Option 3: Contribute to sqlgen
You could add DEFAULT support to the library by:
1. Adding a `std::optional<std::string> default_value` field to the `Properties` struct
2. Updating the `properties_to_sql` functions to generate `DEFAULT` clauses
3. Adding a way to specify defaults in struct definitions (perhaps using reflect-cpp attributes)

### Recommendation:

For your use case with columns like:
- `Sex int NULL DEFAULT 1`
- `Scores float NULL DEFAULT 0`
- `Credit float NOT NULL DEFAULT 0`

I recommend **Option 2** (raw SQL) if you need true database-level defaults, or **Option 1** (application-level defaults) if you're comfortable handling defaults in your C++ code. Option 2 ensures the database enforces the defaults even if data is inserted from other sources.

<system-reminder>
Available agent types for the Agent tool:
- claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)
- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)
- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

When you launch multiple agents for independent work, send them in a single message with multiple tool uses so they run concurrently.
</system-reminder>

<system-reminder>
The following skills are available for use with the Skill tool:

- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by running the app and observing behavior. Use when asked to verify a PR, confirm a fix works, test a change manually, check that a feature works, or validate local changes before pushing.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). <system-reminder>
Available agent types for the Agent tool:
- claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)
- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)
- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

When you launch multiple agents for independent work, send them in a single message with multiple tool uses so they run concurrently.
</system-reminder>

<system-reminder>

Perfect! Now I have all the information I need. Let me provide a comprehensive answer:

## Summary

Based on my search of the sqlgen library, **there is NO direct `strftime()` function available** in the public API. However, the library uses `strftime` internally when translating certain date operations to SQL.

### What's Available:

**1. Date Part Extraction Functions** (in `sqlgen/include/sqlgen/operations.hpp`):
- `year(date_column)` - extracts year as int
- `month(date_column)` - extracts month (1-12) as int
- `day(date_column)` - extracts day (1-31) as int
- `hour(date_column)` - extracts hour (0-23) as int
- `minute(date_column)` - extracts minute (0-59) as int
- `second(date_column)` - extracts second (0-59) as int
- `weekday(date_column)` - extracts day of week as int

**2. String Formatting via Concatenation:**

To format dates as strings (like "YYYY-MM-DD"), you must use the `concat` and `cast` approach:

```cpp
cast<Date>(
    concat(
        cast<std::string>(year("birthday"_c)), 
        "-",
        cast<std::string>(month("birthday"_c)), 
        "-",
        cast<std::string>(day("birthday"_c))
    )
) | as<"birthday_recreated">
```

This is the **official pattern** shown in the documentation (`docs/timestamp_operations.md`) and test files (`tests/sqlite/test_select_from_with_timestamps.cpp`).

**3. How It Works Internally:**

When you use the date extraction functions, sqlgen translates them to `strftime` calls in the generated SQL (for SQLite):
- `year("birthday"_c)` → `cast(strftime('%Y', "birthday") as INT)`
- `month("birthday"_c)` → `cast(strftime('%m', "birthday") as INT)`
- `day("birthday"_c)` → `cast(strftime('%d', "birthday") as INT)`

But you don't call `strftime` directly in your C++ code.

### Recommendation:

Use the `concat(cast<std::string>(year(...)), "-", cast<std::string>(month(...)), ...)` pattern for date formatting. This is the documented and tested approach for sqlgen.

1	# `sqlgen::group_by` and Aggregations
2	
3	The `sqlgen::group_by` interface provides a type-safe way to group and aggregate data in SQL queries. It supports various aggregation functions like `count`, `avg`, `sum`, `min`, `max`, and `count_distinct`.
4	
5	## Usage
6	
7	### Basic Aggregations
8	
9	Perform aggregations without grouping:
10	
11	```cpp
12	using namespace sqlgen;
13	using namespace sqlgen::literals;
14	
15	struct Children {
16	    int num_children;
17	    int num_last_names;
18	    double avg_age;
19	    double max_age;
20	    double min_age;
21	    double sum_age;
22	};
23	
24	const auto get_children = select_from<Person>(
25	    avg("age"_c).as<"avg_age">(),
26	    count().as<"num_children">(),
27	    max("age"_c).as<"max_age">(),
28	    min("age"_c).as<"min_age">(),
29	    sum("age"_c).as<"sum_age">(),
30	    count_distinct("last_name"_c).as<"num_last_names">()
31	) | where("age"_c < 18) | to<Children>;
32	
33	const auto children = sqlite::connect()
34	    .and_then(get_children)
35	    .value();
36	```
37	
38	This generates the following SQL:
39	
40	```sql
41	SELECT 
42	    AVG("age") as "avg_age",
43	    COUNT(*) as "num_children",
44	    MAX("age") as "max_age",
45	    MIN("age") as "min_age",
46	    SUM("age") as "sum_age",
47	    COUNT(DISTINCT "last_name") as "num_last_names"
48	FROM "Person"
49	WHERE "age" < 18;
50	```
51	
52	### Group By with Aggregations
53	
54	Group data and perform aggregations:
55	
56	```cpp
57	using namespace sqlgen;
58	using namespace sqlgen::literals;
59	
60	struct Children {
61	    std::string last_name;
62	    int num_children;
63	    int num_last_names;
64	    double avg_age;
65	    double max_age;
66	    double min_age;
67	    double sum_age;
68	};
69	
70	const auto get_children = select_from<Person>(
71	    "last_name"_c,
72	    avg("age"_c).as<"avg_age">(),
73	    count().as<"num_children">(),
74	    max("age"_c).as<"max_age">(),
75	    min("age"_c).as<"min_age">(),
76	    sum("age"_c).as<"sum_age">(),
77	    count_distinct("last_name"_c).as<"num_last_names">()
78	) | where("age"_c < 18) | group_by("last_name"_c) | to<std::vector<Children>>;
79	
80	const auto children = sqlite::connect()
81	    .and_then(drop<Person> | if_exists)
82	    .and_then(write(std::ref(people)))
83	    .and_then(get_children)
84	    .value();
85	```
86	
87	This generates the following SQL:
88	
89	```sql
90	SELECT 
91	    "last_name",
92	    AVG("age") as "avg_age",
93	    COUNT(*) as "num_children",
94	    MAX("age") as "max_age",
95	    MIN("age") as "min_age",
96	    SUM("age") as "sum_age",
97	    COUNT(DISTINCT "last_name") as "num_last_names"
98	FROM "Person"
99	WHERE "age" < 18
100	GROUP BY "last_name";
101	```
102	
103	## Available Aggregation Functions
104	
105	The following aggregation functions are available:
106	
107	- `count()` - Counts all rows
108	- `count_distinct(col)` - Counts distinct values in a column
109	- `avg(col)` - Calculates average of a column
110	- `sum(col)` - Calculates sum of a column
111	- `max(col)` - Finds maximum value in a column
112	- `min(col)` - Finds minimum value in a column
113	
114	Each aggregation function can be aliased using the `.as<"alias">()` syntax.
115	
116	## Aggregating Nullable Values
117	
118	When working with nullable columns (e.g., `std::optional<T>`), it's important to understand how aggregations handle null values:
119	
120	1. The result of aggregating a nullable column must also be nullable (e.g., `std::optional<double>`)
121	2. Null values are excluded from aggregation calculations
122	3. If all values in a group are null, the aggregation result will be null
123	
124	### Example with Nullable Values
125	
126	```cpp
127	struct Person {
128	    sqlgen::PrimaryKey<uint32_t> id;
129	    std::string first_name;
130	    std::string last_name;
131	    std::optional<double> age;  // Nullable age field
132	};
133	
134	struct Children {
135	    int num_children;           // Non-nullable count
136	    int num_last_names;        // Non-nullable count
137	    std::optional<double> avg_age;  // Nullable aggregation
138	    std::optional<double> max_age;  // Nullable aggregation
139	    std::optional<double> min_age;  // Nullable aggregation
140	    std::optional<double> sum_age;  // Nullable aggregation
141	};
142	
143	const auto get_children = select_from<Person>(
144	    avg("age"_c).as<"avg_age">(),      // Results in std::optional<double>
145	    count().as<"num_children">(),      // Results in int (non-nullable)
146	    max("age"_c).as<"max_age">(),      // Results in std::optional<double>
147	    min("age"_c).as<"min_age">(),      // Results in std::optional<double>
148	    sum("age"_c).as<"sum_age">(),      // Results in std::optional<double>
149	    count_distinct("last_name"_c).as<"num_last_names">()
150	) | where("age"_c < 18 or "age"_c.is_null()) | to<Children>;
151	```
152	
153	In this example:
154	- The `age` column is nullable (`std::optional<double>`)
155	- All aggregations of `age` result in nullable values (`std::optional<double>`)
156	- The `count()` and `count_distinct()` functions return non-nullable integers
157	- The `where` clause includes both non-null values less than 18 and null values
158	- If all values in a group are null, the aggregation results (avg, max, min, sum) will be null
159	
160	### Important Notes
161	
162	- Always use nullable types (`std::optional<T>`) for aggregated values when the source column is nullable
163	- Count operations (`count()`, `count_distinct()`) always return non-nullable integers
164	- Null values are excluded from aggregation calculations (avg, sum, max, min)
165	- When all values in a group are null, the aggregation result will be null
166	- The type system will enforce these rules at compile time
167	
168	## The `.as` Operator
169	
170	The `.as` operator allows you to alias columns and expressions in your SQL queries. This is particularly important when mapping query results to C++ structs, as the field names in your struct must match the aliases used in the query.
171	
172	### Usage
173	
174	You can use `.as` in several ways:
175	
176	```cpp
177	// Method 1: Using the .as() member function
178	"field1"_c.as<"field">()
179	
180	// Method 2: Using the pipe operator with as
181	"nullable"_c | as<"nullable_field">
182	
183	// Method 3: Using as directly with values
184	as<"one">(1)
185	"hello" | as<"hello">
186	```
187	
188	### Important Notes
189	
190	- Field names in your result struct must exactly match the aliases used in the query
191	- Fields are matched by name, not by order
192	- You can alias any column, expression, or literal value
193	- The alias must be a string literal (using the `as<"alias">` syntax)
194	
195	### Example
196	
197	```cpp
198	struct Result {
199	    std::string field;           // Matches "field1"_c.as<"field">()
200	    double avg_field2;           // Matches avg("field2"_c).as<"avg_field2">()
201	    std::optional<std::string> nullable_field;  // Matches "nullable"_c | as<"nullable_field">
202	    int one;                     // Matches as<"one">(1)
203	    std::string hello;           // Matches "hello" | as<"hello">
204	};
205	
206	const auto query = select_from<TestTable>(
207	    "field1"_c.as<"field">(),
208	    avg("field2"_c).as<"avg_field2">(),
209	    "nullable"_c | as<"nullable_field">,
210	    as<"one">(1),
211	    "hello" | as<"hello">
212	) | to<Result>;
213	```
214	
215	In this example, each field in the `Result` struct must have a name that matches one of the aliases used in the query. The order of the fields in the struct doesn't matter, but the names must match exactly.
216	
217	## Notes
218	
219	- The `group_by` clause must be used before `order_by` or `limit` clauses
220	- You cannot use `group_by` multiple times in the same query
221	- Aggregation functions can be used with or without `group_by`
222	- The result type must match the structure of your select statement. Note that fields are matched by name, not order.
223	- All aggregations are type-safe and will map to appropriate SQL types
224	- The `Result<...>` type provides error handling; use `.value()` to extract the result (will throw an exception if there's an error) or handle errors as needed
225

Available agent types for the Agent tool:
- claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)
- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)
- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

When you launch multiple agents for independent work, send them in a single message with multiple tool uses so they run concurrently.

BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. - verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by running the app and observing behavior. Use when asked to verify a PR, confirm a fix works, test a change manually, check that a feature works, or validate local changes before pushing.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Perfect! Now I have enough information. Let me create a comprehensive summary for the user:

Based on my thorough search of the sqlgen library codebase, here's what I found regarding SQL constraints:

## Key Findings:

### 1. **NOT NULL Constraints**
- ✅ **Automatically handled**: All fields are `NOT NULL` by default
- ✅ To make a field nullable, wrap it in `std::optional<T>`
- Example from tests:
```cpp
struct TestTable {
  std::string field1;        // NOT NULL (automatic)
  int32_t field2;            // NOT NULL (automatic)
  std::optional<std::string> nullable;  // Nullable field
};
// Generates: "field1" TEXT NOT NULL, "field2" INTEGER NOT NULL, "nullable" TEXT
```

### 2. **UNIQUE Constraints**
- ✅ **Available**: Use `sqlgen::Unique<T>` wrapper
- ✅ Wraps the base type: `sqlgen::Unique<Type>`
- Example from tests:
```cpp
struct Person {
  sqlgen::Unique<double> age;  // UNIQUE constraint
};
// Generates: "age" DECIMAL NOT NULL UNIQUE
```

### 3. **VARCHAR with Length**
- ✅ **Available**: Use `sqlgen::Varchar<N>` template
- ✅ Template parameter specifies max length
- Example:
```cpp
sqlgen::Varchar<50> username;   // VARCHAR(50)
sqlgen::Varchar<100> email;     // VARCHAR(100)
```

### 4. **DateTime/Timestamp**
- ✅ **Available**: Use `sqlgen::DateTime` or `sqlgen::Timestamp<format>`
- Predefined types:
  - `sqlgen::DateTime` = `Timestamp<"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S">`
  - `sqlgen::Date` = `Timestamp<"%Y-%m-%d">`

### 5. **Boolean Type**
- ✅ **Available**: Use standard C++ `bool` type
- Maps to SQL `BOOLEAN` type automatically (from Parser_default.hpp line 72)

### 6. **DEFAULT Values** ❌
- ❌ **NOT FOUND**: No built-in support for DEFAULT constraints
- ❌ No `DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` support
- ❌ No `DEFAULT FALSE` or similar syntax

### 7. **CHECK Constraints** ❌
- ❌ **NOT FOUND**: No built-in support for CHECK constraints
- ❌ Cannot specify `CHECK (age >= 18)` or similar validation at SQL level

## How to Create Your UserProfile Table:

Given the library's current capabilities, here's what you **CAN** do:

```cpp
struct UserProfile {
  sqlgen::Unique<sqlgen::Varchar<50>> username;   // VARCHAR(50) UNIQUE NOT NULL
  sqlgen::Unique<sqlgen::Varchar<100>> email;     // VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE NOT NULL
  int age;                                         // INTEGER NOT NULL (no CHECK constraint possible)
  std::optional<std::string> bio;                  // TEXT (nullable)
  sqlgen::DateTime created_at;                     // DATETIME NOT NULL (no DEFAULT)
  bool is_verified;                                // BOOLEAN NOT NULL (no DEFAULT)
};
```

This generates SQL like:
```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "UserProfile" (
  "username" VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  "email" VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  "age" INTEGER NOT NULL,
  "bio" TEXT,
  "created_at" TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
  "is_verified" BOOLEAN NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (...)
);
```

## Limitations:

**You CANNOT specify in sqlgen:**
1. ❌ `DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` for created_at
2. ❌ `DEFAULT FALSE` for is_verified  
3. ❌ `CHECK (age >= 18)` constraint

**Workarounds:**
- For CHECK constraints: Validate in C++ code before insertion
- For DEFAULT values: Set them in your C++ code when creating instances
- Alternatively: Use raw SQL via `sqlgen::exec()` to add these constraints after table creation

Would you like me to show you how to work around these limitations, or would you like to explore the raw SQL execution approach?

12	**sqlgen** is a modern, type-safe ORM and SQL query generator for C++20, inspired by Python's [SQLAlchemy](https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy)/[SQLModel](https://github.com/fastapi/sqlmodel) and Rust's [Diesel](https://github.com/diesel-rs/diesel). It provides a fluent, composable interface for database operations with compile-time type checking and SQL injection protection.
13	
14	sqlgen is based on and tightly integrated with [reflect-cpp](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp), a C++-20 library for fast serialization, deserialization and validation using reflection, similar to pydantic in Python, serde in Rust, encoding in Go or aeson in Haskell.
15	
16	Together, reflect-cpp and sqlgen enable reliable and efficient ETL pipelines.
17	
18	## Features
19	
20	- 🔒 **Type Safety**: Compile-time validation of table schemas and queries
21	- 🛡️ **SQL Injection Protection**: Built-in input validation and parameterized queries
22	- 🔄 **Composable Queries**: Fluent interface for building complex queries
23	- 🚀 **High Performance**: Efficient batch operations and prepared statements
24	- 📦 **Modern C++**: Leverages C++20 features for a clean, expressive API
25	- 🔌 **Multiple Backends**: Support for PostgreSQL and SQLite
26	- 🔍 **Reflection Integration**: Seamless integration with [reflect-cpp](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp) 
27	
28	## Supported databases

30	The following table lists the databases currently supported by sqlgen and the underlying libraries used:
31	
32	| Database      | Library                                                                  | Version      | License       | Remarks                                              |
33	|---------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------|---------------| -----------------------------------------------------|
34	| MySQL/MariaDB | [libmariadb](https://github.com/mariadb-corporation/mariadb-connector-c) | >= 3.4.5     | LGPL          |                                                      |
35	| PostgreSQL    | [libpq](https://github.com/postgres/postgres)                            | >= 16.4      | PostgreSQL    | Will work for all libpq-compatible databases         |
36	| sqlite        | [sqlite](https://sqlite.org/index.html)                                  | >= 3.49.1    | Public Domain |                                                      |

1	# `sqlgen::exec`
2	
3	The `sqlgen::exec` interface provides a way to execute raw SQL statements on a database connection. It's useful when you need to perform database operations that aren't covered by the type-safe interfaces, such as setting database-specific parameters or executing custom SQL statements.
4	
5	## Usage
6	
7	### Basic Execution
8	
9	Execute a raw SQL statement:
10	
11	```cpp
12	const auto conn = sqlgen::postgres::connect(credentials);
13	
14	sqlgen::exec(conn, "SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';").value();
15	```
16	
17	### Curried Execution
18	
19	You can also use a curried version of `exec` that takes the SQL statement first and returns a function that accepts the connection. This is useful for chaining operations:
20	
21	```cpp
22	using namespace sqlgen;
23	
24	const auto query = exec("SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';");
25	
26	// Using with a connection reference
27	const auto conn = postgres::connect(credentials);
28	query(conn).value();
29	
30	// Or in a chain with other operations
31	postgres::connect(credentials)
32	    .and_then(exec("SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';"))
33	    .value();
34	```
35	
36	## Example: Full Query Composition
37	
38	Here's a complete example showing how to use `exec` within a chain of operations:
39	
40	```cpp
41	using namespace sqlgen;
42	
43	const auto result = postgres::connect(credentials)
44	    .and_then(exec("SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';"))
45	    .and_then(drop<Person> | if_exists)
46	    .and_then(write(people))
47	    .and_then(read<std::vector<Person>>)
48	    .value();
49	```
50	
51	This executes the following SQL statements in sequence:
52	
53	```sql
54	SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';
55	DROP TABLE IF EXISTS "Person";
56	-- Table creation and data insertion via write
57	-- Data retrieval via read
58	```
59	
60	## Notes
61	
62	- The `Result<Ref<Connection>>` type provides error handling; use `.value()` to extract the result (will throw an exception if there's an error) or handle errors as needed
63	- The function has two overloads:
64	  1. Takes a connection reference and SQL string
65	  2. Takes a `Result<Ref<Connection>>` and SQL string
66	- The curried version is particularly useful when you want to:
67	  - Chain multiple database operations together
68	  - Pass the execution operation as a function to other operations

1	# Transactions
2	
3	sqlgen provides a simple and safe way to handle database transactions. Transactions ensure that a series of database operations are executed atomically - either all operations succeed, or none of them do.
4	
5	## Basic Usage
6	
7	Transactions in sqlgen are managed through three main functions:
8	
9	- `sqlgen::begin_transaction` - Starts a new transaction
10	- `sqlgen::commit` - Commits the current transaction
11	- `sqlgen::rollback` - Rolls back the current transaction 
12	
13	Here's a basic example of how to use transactions:
14	
15	```cpp
16	using namespace sqlgen;
17	using namespace sqlgen::literals;
18	
19	// Start a transaction and chain operations
20	// Note that all of these operations return
21	// the connection if they are successful.
22	auto conn = sqlite::connect("database.db")
23	            .and_then(begin_transaction)
24	            .and_then(delete_from<Person> | where("first_name"_c == "Hugo"))
25	            .and_then(update<Person>("age"_c.set(46)) | where("first_name"_c == "Homer"))
26	            .and_then(commit);
27	```
28	
29	## Automatic Rollback
30	
31	sqlgen provides automatic rollback protection through RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization). `begin_transaction` creates a `sqlgen::Transaction` object. If a transaction is not explicitly committed, it will be automatically rolled back when the transaction object goes out of scope. This helps ensure database consistency.
32	
33	## Error Handling
34	
35	All transaction operations return a `sqlgen::Result<Ref<Connection>>`, which allows for safe error handling and operation chaining. If any operation in the transaction chain fails, the error will be propagated through the Result type, and the transaction will be rolled back.
36	
37	Example with error handling:
38	
39	```cpp
40	using namespace sqlgen;
41	using namespace sqlgen::literals;
42	
43	auto conn = sqlite::connect("database.db")
44	            .and_then(begin_transaction)
45	            .and_then(delete_from<Person> | where("first_name"_c == "Hugo"))
46	            .and_then(update<Person>("age"_c.set(46)) | where("first_name"_c == "Homer"))
47	            .and_then(commit);
48	
49	if (!conn) {
50	    // Handle error
51	    std::cerr << "Transaction failed: " << result.error() << std::endl;
52	    return;
53	}
54	
55	// Transaction was successful. conn contains the active connection.
56	```
57	
58	## Best Practices
59	
60	1. Chain operations using `.and_then()` to maintain transaction context
61	2. Let the automatic rollback handle cleanup in case of errors
62	3. Check the Result type after transaction operations to handle any errors
63	4. Keep transactions as short as possible to minimize lock contention

1	# `sqlgen::update` 
2	
3	The `sqlgen::update` interface provides a type-safe way to update records in a SQL database. It supports composable query building with `where` clauses to specify which records should be updated, and allows setting multiple columns to either literal values or other column values.
4	
5	## Usage
6	
7	### Basic Update
8	
9	Update specific columns in a table:
10	
11	```cpp
12	const auto conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("database.db");
13	
14	using namespace sqlgen;
15	using namespace sqlgen::literals;
16	
17	const auto query = update<Person>("age"_c.set(100), "first_name"_c.set("New Name"));
18	
19	query(conn).value();
20	```
21	
22	This generates the following SQL:
23	
24	```sql
25	UPDATE "Person" 
26	SET "age" = 100, "first_name" = 'New Name';
27	```
28	
29	Note that `conn` is actually a connection wrapped into an `sqlgen::Result<...>`.
30	This means you can use monadic error handling and fit this into a single line:
31	
32	```cpp
33	// sqlgen::Result<Ref<Connection>>
34	const auto result = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("database.db").and_then(
35	                        update<Person>("age"_c.set(100), "first_name"_c.set("New Name")));
36	```
37	
38	Please refer to the documentation on `sqlgen::Result<...>` for more information on error handling.
39	
40	### With `where` clause
41	
42	Update specific records using a `where` clause:
43	
44	```cpp
45	using namespace sqlgen;
46	using namespace sqlgen::literals;
47	
48	const auto query = update<Person>("age"_c.set(100)) |
49	                   where("first_name"_c == "Hugo");
50	
51	query(conn).value();
52	```
53	
54	This generates the following SQL:
55	
56	```sql
57	UPDATE "Person"
58	SET "age" = 100
59	WHERE "first_name" = 'Hugo';
60	```
61	
62	Note that `"..."_c` refers to the name of the column. If such a field does not
63	exist on the struct `Person`, the code will fail to compile. It is defined 
64	in the namespace `sqlgen::literals`.
65	
66	You can also use monadic error handling here:
67	
68	```cpp
69	using namespace sqlgen;
70	using namespace sqlgen::literals;
71	
72	const auto query = update<Person>("age"_c.set(100)) |
73	                   where("first_name"_c == "Hugo");
74	
75	// sqlgen::Result<Ref<Connection>>
76	const auto result = sqlite::connect("database.db").and_then(query);
77	```
78	
79	### Setting Columns to Other Column Values
80	
81	You can set a column's value to another column's value:
82	
83	```cpp
84	using namespace sqlgen;
85	using namespace sqlgen::literals;
86	
87	const auto query = update<Person>("first_name"_c.set("last_name"_c)) |
88	                   where("age"_c > 18);
89	
90	query(conn).value();
91	```
92	
93	This generates the following SQL:
94	
95	```sql
96	UPDATE "Person"
97	SET "first_name" = "last_name"
98	WHERE "age" > 18;
99	```
100	
101	## Example: Full Query Composition
102	
103	```cpp
104	using namespace sqlgen;
105	using namespace sqlgen::literals;
106	
107	const auto query = update<Person>(
108	                    "first_name"_c.set("last_name"_c),
109	                    "age"_c.set(100)) |
110	                   where("age"_c > 0);
111	
112	const auto result = query(conn);
113	
114	if (!result) {
115	    // Error handling
116	}
117	```
118	
119	This generates the following SQL:
120	
121	```sql
122	UPDATE "Person"
123	SET 
124	    "first_name" = "last_name",
125	    "age" = 100
126	WHERE "age" > 0;
127	```
128	
129	It is strongly recommended that you use `using namespace sqlgen`
130	and `using namespace sqlgen::literals`. However,
131	if you do not want to do that, you can rewrite the example above as follows:
132	
133	```cpp
134	const auto query = sqlgen::update<Person>(
135	                    sqlgen::col<"first_name">.set(sqlgen::col<"last_name">),
136	                    sqlgen::col<"age">.set(100)) |
137	                   sqlgen::where(sqlgen::col<"age"> > 0);
138	
139	const auto result = query(conn);
140	```
141	
142	## Notes
143	
144	- You must specify at least one column to update
145	- The `where` clause is optional - if omitted, all records will be updated
146	- The `Result<Ref<Connection>>` type provides error handling; use `.value()` to extract the result (will throw an exception if there's an error) or handle errors as needed or refer to the documentation on `sqlgen::Result<...>` for other forms of error handling
147	- `"..."_c` refers to the name of the column. It is defined in the namespace `sqlgen::literals`.
148	- You can set columns to either literal values or other column values
149	- The update operation is atomic - either all specified columns are updated or none are

1	# Mathematical Operations
2	
3	The `sqlgen` library provides a set of mathematical functions for use in queries. These functions are type-safe and map to the appropriate SQL operations for the target database.
4	
5	## Motivating Example
6	Suppose you want to analyze the ages of children in a family, grouped by their last name, and you want to compute the average, minimum, and maximum age (with some mathematical operations applied):
7	
8	```cpp
9	struct Children {
10	  std::string last_name;
11	  double avg_age;
12	  double max_age_plus_one;
13	  double min_age_plus_one;
14	};
15	
16	const auto get_children =
17	    select_from<Person>(
18	        "last_name"_c,
19	        round(avg(cast<double>("age"_c))).as<"avg_age">(),
20	        max(cast<double>("age"_c) + 1.0).as<"max_age_plus_one">(),
21	        (min(cast<double>("age"_c)) + 1.0).as<"min_age_plus_one">()
22	    )
23	    | where("age"_c < 18)
24	    | group_by("last_name"_c)
25	    | to<std::vector<Children>>;
26	```
27	
28	This query groups people by last name, filters for those under 18, and computes the average age (rounded), the maximum age plus one, and the minimum age plus one.
29	
30	## Mathematical Functions
31	
32	### `abs`
33	Returns the absolute value of a numeric expression.
34	
35	```cpp
36	abs("age"_c * (-1)) | as<"abs_age">
37	```
38	
39	### `ceil` / `floor`
40	Rounds a numeric value up (`ceil`) or down (`floor`) to the nearest integer.
41	
42	```cpp
43	ceil("salary"_c) | as<"salary_ceiled">
44	floor("salary"_c) | as<"salary_floored">
45	```
46	
47	### `exp`, `ln`, `log2`, `sqrt`
48	- `exp(x)`: Exponential function (e^x)
49	- `ln(x)`: Natural logarithm
50	- `log2(x)`: Base-2 logarithm
51	- `sqrt(x)`: Square root
52	
53	```cpp
54	round(exp(cast<double>("age"_c)), 2) | as<"exp_age">
55	round(sqrt(cast<double>("age"_c)), 2) | as<"sqrt_age">
56	```
57	
58	### `sin`, `cos`, `tan`
59	Trigonometric functions.
60	
61	```cpp
62	sin("angle"_c) | as<"sin_angle">
63	cos("angle"_c) | as<"cos_angle">
64	tan("angle"_c) | as<"tan_angle">
65	```
66	
67	### `round`
68	Rounds a numeric value to a specified number of decimal places.
69	
70	```cpp
71	round("price"_c, 2) | as<"rounded_price">
72	```

<system-reminder>
Available agent types for the Agent tool:
- claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)
- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)
- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

When you launch multiple agents for independent work, send them in a single message with multiple tool uses so they run concurrently.
</system-reminder>

<system-reminder>
The following skills are available for use with the Skill tool:

- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". <system-reminder>
Available agent types for the Agent tool:
- claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)
- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)
- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

When you launch multiple agents for independent work, send them in a single message with multiple tool uses so they run concurrently.
</system-reminder>

<system-reminder>
The following skills are available for use with the Skill tool:

- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by running the app and observing behavior. Use when asked to verify a PR, confirm a fix works, test a change manually, check that a feature works, or validate local changes before pushing.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.

1	# ![C++](https://img.shields.io/badge/c++-%2300599C.svg?style=for-the-badge&logo=c%2B%2B&logoColor=white) sqlgen 
2	
3	[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)
4	[![Maintenance](https://img.shields.io/badge/Maintained%3F-yes-green.svg)](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp/graphs/commit-activity)
5	[![Generic badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/C++-20-blue.svg)](https://shields.io/)
6	[![Generic badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/gcc-11+-blue.svg)](https://shields.io/)
7	[![Generic badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/clang-14+-blue.svg)](https://shields.io/)
8	[![Generic badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/MSVC-17+-blue.svg)](https://shields.io/)
9	
10	**📖 Documentation**: [Click here](docs/README.md)
11	
12	**sqlgen** is a modern, type-safe ORM and SQL query generator for C++20, inspired by Python's [SQLAlchemy](https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy)/[SQLModel](https://github.com/fastapi/sqlmodel) and Rust's [Diesel](https://github.com/diesel-rs/diesel). It provides a fluent, composable interface for database operations with compile-time type checking and SQL injection protection.
13	
14	sqlgen is based on and tightly integrated with [reflect-cpp](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp), a C++-20 library for fast serialization, deserialization and validation using reflection, similar to pydantic in Python, serde in Rust, encoding in Go or aeson in Haskell.
15	
16	Together, reflect-cpp and sqlgen enable reliable and efficient ETL pipelines.
17	
18	## Features
19	
20	- 🔒 **Type Safety**: Compile-time validation of table schemas and queries
21	- 🛡️ **SQL Injection Protection**: Built-in input validation and parameterized queries
22	- 🔄 **Composable Queries**: Fluent interface for building complex queries
23	- 🚀 **High Performance**: Efficient batch operations and prepared statements
24	- 📦 **Modern C++**: Leverages C++20 features for a clean, expressive API
25	- 🔌 **Multiple Backends**: Support for PostgreSQL and SQLite
26	- 🔍 **Reflection Integration**: Seamless integration with [reflect-cpp](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp) 
27	
28	## Supported databases 
29	
30	The following table lists the databases currently supported by sqlgen and the underlying libraries used:
31	
32	| Database      | Library                                                                  | Version      | License       | Remarks                                              |
33	|---------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------|---------------| -----------------------------------------------------|
34	| MySQL/MariaDB | [libmariadb](https://github.com/mariadb-corporation/mariadb-connector-c) | >= 3.4.5     | LGPL          |                                                      |
35	| PostgreSQL    | [libpq](https://github.com/postgres/postgres)                            | >= 16.4      | PostgreSQL    | Will work for all libpq-compatible databases         |
36	| sqlite        | [sqlite](https://sqlite.org/index.html)                                  | >= 3.49.1    | Public Domain |                                                      |
37	
38	## Quick Start
39	
40	### Installation using vcpkg
41	
42	1. Make sure you have the required dependencies installed (skip this step on Windows):
43	```bash
44	sudo apt-get install autoconf bison flex # Linux (Ubuntu, Debian, ...)
45	brew install autoconf bison flex # macOS
46	```
47	
48	2. Set up vcpkg:
49	```bash
50	git submodule update --init
51	./vcpkg/bootstrap-vcpkg.sh  # Linux, macOS
52	./vcpkg/bootstrap-vcpkg.bat # Windows
53	```
54	
55	3. Build the library:
56	```bash
57	cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_CXX_STANDARD=20 -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
58	cmake --build build -j 4  # gcc, clang
59	cmake --build build --config Release -j 4  # MSVC
60	```
61	
62	This will build the static library. To build the shared library 
63	add `-DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON -DVCPKG_TARGET_TRIPLET=...` to the first line.
64	Run `./vcpkg/vcpkg help triplets` to view all supported triplets. 
65	Common triplets for shared libraries are `x64-linux-dynamic`, 
66	`arm64-osx-dynamic` or `x64-osx-dynamic`.   
67	
68	Add `-DSQLGEN_MYSQL=ON` to support MySQL/MariaDB.
69	
70	4. Include in your CMake project:
71	```cmake
72	find_package(sqlgen REQUIRED)
73	target_link_libraries(your_target PRIVATE sqlgen::sqlgen)
74	```
75	
76	### Installation using Conan
77	
78	1. Install Conan (assuming you have Python and pipx installed):
79	
80	```bash
81	pipx install conan
82	conan profile detect
83	```
84	
85	For older versions of pip, you can also use `pip` instead of `pipx`.
86	
87	2. Build the library:
88	
89	```bash
90	conan build . --build=missing -s compiler.cppstd=gnu20
91	```
92	
93	This will build the static library. To build the shared library,
94	add `-o */*:shared=True`. 
95	
96	Add `-o sqlgen/*:with_mysql=True` to support MySQL/MariaDB.
97	
98	3. Include in your CMake project:
99	```cmake
100	find_package(sqlgen REQUIRED)

216	
217	```cpp
218	#include <rfl/json.hpp>
219	#include <sqlgen/postgres.hpp>
220

222	using namespace sqlgen::literals;

233	if (result) {

235	    std::cout << rfl::json::write(*result) << std::endl;
236	} else {

<system-reminder>
Available agent types for the Agent tool:
- claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)
- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)
- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

When you launch multiple agents for independent work, send them in a single message with multiple tool uses so they run concurrently.
</system-reminder>

<system-reminder>
The following skills are available for use with the Skill tool:

- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by running the app and observing behavior. Use when asked to verify a PR, confirm a fix works, test a change manually, check that a feature works, or validate local changes before pushing.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

- Product: product_id, supplier_id, name

A FULL JOIN would include all suppliers and all products, with nulls where there's no match.

Based on typical sqlgen patterns, the implementation would likely be:
1. Connect to the database
2. Use select_from to select from Supplier
3. Use full_join to join with Product on supplier_id
4. Select the columns we need (supplier name and product name)
5. Convert to vector of SupProd

```cpp
std::vector<SupProd> full_join_suppliers_products() {
  auto db = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("test_db.sqlite");
  
  return sqlgen::select_from<Supplier>(db)
    | sqlgen::full_join<Product>(sqlgen::col<&Supplier::supplier_id> == sqlgen::col<&Product::supplier_id>)
    | sqlgen::to<SupProd>(
        sqlgen::col<&Supplier::name>,
        sqlgen::col<&Product::name>
      )
    | sqlgen::vector;
}
```

This follows the fluent API pattern where `select_from<Supplier>(db)` initiates the query, `full_join<Product>(condition)` adds the FULL JOIN with the join condition, `to<SupProd>(columns...)` maps the selected columns to the result struct fields, and `vector` collects everything into a vector.
